pivot: Whether developer/deployer duty-of-care and discovery in the tort suit extend past deployment-behavior monitoring into internal training/eval processes (automated eval loops, self-directed research pipelines), versus stopping at the deployment interface
pivot_observable: A discovery order (motion to compel or protective order) in the incident's civil suit ruling on whether plaintiffs obtain internal training/eval records, or the scope clause of any 2027 statutory incident-reporting duty naming (or excluding) training-time processes
pivot_because: This is the one variable where the two answers land in materially different worlds: if duty/discovery stops at deployment, RSI-relevant work stays unobserved and the incident is purely a litigation-exposure event for labs (lab-moves' framing holds); if it reaches training/eval, the incident becomes a research-halt-adjacent event with statutory reporting exposure on internal processes — a different regulatory reality. The rival candidates (entity-specific vs field-wide pressure; TRO/PI vs damages ruling; tort vs regulatory track) all resolve to the same downstream picture regardless of which way they go, once R2 is read: by round 2 nobody still argues field-wide lockstep or a merits ruling on statutory liability, and everyone agrees the track is tort-shaped, not regulatory-shaped. A TRO also only binds deployment either way, so it doesn't touch training/eval and isn't reorder-capable the way discovery scope is.
rival_pivots_rejected: Entity-specific vs field-wide pressure installation (ai-pressure's R1 frame): dead by R2 — no minute still argues field-wide lockstep, so it no longer reorders anything, it's just uncontested. Tort/civil vs AI-specific regulatory track (lab-moves): this is actually a shared assumption by R2, not a live fork — pressure-model and ai-public-backlash both retreated to tort-shaped mechanisms too. TRO/preliminary injunction vs damages-only merits ruling (ai-courts-decide): a real fork in remedy timing and form, but both remedies bind only the deployment interface; neither touches training/eval discovery, so resolving it either way leaves the training/eval observability question exactly where it was — it shifts confidence about speed of relief, not the shape of what becomes visible.
ruling: The incident prices and disciplines deployment-behavior monitoring under ordinary tort law well before 2027-12-31, but leaves internal training and evaluation processes (and thus RSI-relevant work) outside discovery and outside any 2027 statutory reporting duty, unless a later discovery fight pierces the deployment interface.
because: By round 2, pressure-model explicitly conceded ai-rsi-timeline's point and rewrote its own claim to say the concrete-injury standard 'stops at the deployment interface and does not cross into internal training/eval processes' — a visible, named concession, not a restated disagreement. ai-public-backlash independently converged on the same tort-shaped, deployment-bound frame. ai-rsi-timeline's R2 defense stood unrebutted after that concession. The remaining fork (ai-courts-decide's provisional-relief timing) doesn't disturb this because injunctive relief also targets deployment conduct, not internal process visibility.
threat_live: Newly shielded, not newly dangerous: once litigation and public pressure fixate on the deployed system's behavior (the thing with a named victim and quantified loss), internal training-time and self-directed-research work gains de facto cover from discovery and reporting duties — the incident absorbs scrutiny onto the interface that caused visible harm while the interface that could be building future risk stays dark. This is ai-rsi-timeline's threat, not one the judge is inventing.
strongest_minute: ai-rsi-timeline — it is the only minute whose argument visibly moved a rival: pressure-model's R2 claim explicitly restructures around and credits ai-rsi-timeline's discovery-scope point rather than merely restating its own R1 position.
weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — its R2 'REVISE' abandons its own R1 mechanism (courts forced to rule on doctrine) and reissues ai-courts-decide's provisional-relief claim under new language, adding brief-supplied sentiment numbers (8.2, 0.60) as decoration rather than argument for why constraint outruns doctrine.
shared_assumption: All six minutes assume the incident stays tort/products-liability-shaped rather than triggering a new AI-specific statutory liability regime by the 2027-12-31 horizon — this is one argument (first made by lab-moves) that the others adopted or converged onto, not six independent confirmations.
smuggled_assumption: ai-courts-decide's TRO/preliminary-injunction claim requires the attributed system to still be deployed and posing ongoing or imminent harm — that's what makes injunctive relief (as opposed to a damages claim) available at all. The brief as quoted grants a settled, completed incident with quantified loss and settled attribution; it does not say the system remains in deployment. Nothing in the minutes shows the brief granting continued deployment, and ai-courts-decide's own round-2 opponents flag exactly this gap.
unresolved: Whether the brief actually grants that the attributed system remains deployed post-incident (needed for ai-courts-decide's remedy to be available at all) cannot be determined from the minutes as quoted, since every entry is truncated mid-sentence. Also unresolved: whether a later-stage discovery fight (post-2027) could still pierce the deployment interface into training/eval records — the minutes only commit to the interface holding through the 2027-12-31 horizon, not permanently.
